S.FORM: Na sususrig / Na susrig sur o m̄erm̄er s-rō valrēg i tbirār.
S.TRANSL: This is the story of two boys and their grandfather.

S.FORM: Tuar qōn̄ nen̄, nēr t-togtog ti, i tbirār m-van a ōt.
S.TRANSL: One day, as they were home, their grandfather went to work in his taro garden.

S.FORM: M-van a ōt, alē rār m-la nāvsirār, rār m-siw le naw, rār t-venven o ninti law ti.
S.TRANSL: While he was in the garden, the two boys took their bows and arrows, walked down to the lagoon, and began fishing for small blennies.

S.FORM: Rār m-venven o ninti law nen̄ avvan, rār m-mōl ma i vre, i tbirār m-mōl ma a ōt, rār m-la ma namirār o law nen̄, tōlnēr so gān.
S.TRANSL: Once they had caught enough blennies, they returned to their hamlet. When their grandfather came back home, they showed him their catch, and everyone had dinner together.

S.FORM: La tōlnēr t-gān qarqar wor ti. 🌿
S.TRANSL: They were just eating their food raw. 🌿

S.FORM: Me-mmat ror, tbirār so van mlē a ōt.
S.TRANSL: The next morning, their grandfather went to the taro garden again.

S.FORM: Ni ron̄ “Ra tbuk, kmur m-togtog, kmur kak m-vanvan le naw wa, kmur vte vanvan te kēl vak gin tuar o wren̄ra; kmur vte vanvan tvilag te vak.
S.TRANSL: But before he left, he told them: “Listen, children. If ever, later today, you walk down to the sea, then make sure you don’t go in that direction over there, to one of those headlands. Make sure you don’t go beyond that point!

S.FORM: Tekgor kmur s-van aē, kmur s-van wōn i tbikmur.”
S.TRANSL: If you ever go there, you might run into one of your ancestors.”

S.FORM: Rār m-van mlē le naw me-tur nāvsirār, rār m-van ror, rār so venven o ninti o law.
S.TRANSL: So off they went again to the coast, with their bows and arrows in hand, until they reached the sea and began to fish for blennies again.

S.FORM: Rār m-venven nen̄ avvan, rār so van vga vak gin tuar o wren̄ra.
S.TRANSL: They went on and on fishing, until they crossed a point.

S.FORM: Bas, rār so mōl ma i vre, tbirār m-mōl nok ma a ōt, tbirār so vārus rār; ron̄ “Kmur m-dēn̄ ave?”
S.TRANSL: And then they returned back home. Their grandfather, who had already come back from the garden, enquired “How far did you go?”

S.FORM: Ron̄ “Kmār m-dēn̄ gin o wren̄ra, kmār so van vak, kmār so van vasul mlē vak gin tuar o wren̄ra.”
S.TRANSL: “Well, after we reached the headland, we pushed a little further, until we reached a second headland.”

S.FORM: Tbirār ron̄ “Kmur gēn m-bas wor t'aē nen̄! Tekgor kmur s-van galāg mlē vak, kmur s-van wōn i tbikmur.” 🌿
S.TRANSL: “Alright – he replied – that’s enough! Take care not to go any further that way, otherwise you’ll run into one of your ancestors!” 🌿

S.FORM: Me-mmat ror le rorwor, rār m-van mlē le naw, tbirār so van mlē a ōt.
S.TRANSL: As they woke up the next morning, the two boys went down to the sea again, while their grandfather went away to the garden.

S.FORM: Rār m-van ror nen̄ le naw, rār m-venven o law, avvan, rār ron̄ “Dār van sē vak sa? Tbidār t-wes gor dār dēn vanvan vak sa ti sur sa?”
S.TRANSL: They walked down to the lagoon and began fishing for blennies. At some point, they said to each other “Can’t we go further up? After all, why does Grandpa forbid us to go this way?”

S.FORM: Rār m-van vak, rār t-ven o law ti, rār m-ron̄ wor sē: o magte so siol dēn ma lēlē lē.
S.TRANSL: So they crossed that point and continued to fish. Then suddenly they heard some rustling: it was an old woman dragging herself out of her cave.

S.FORM: Ron̄ “Kmur t-ven o sav ti?” Ron̄ “O law. Ngatōlkma ra tbikmār.”
S.TRANSL: “What are you fishing for?”, she asked. “Blennies”, they replied. “For the two of us, and for our Grandpa.”

S.FORM: O magte nen̄ ron̄ “Ngatōlgēn!”
S.TRANSL: “Let’s eat them together!” said the old woman.

S.FORM: M-van ma sur rār nen̄, m-la dēn rār o law, ron̄ “Kmur t-gān aksav ti?”
S.TRANSL: She came closer to them, took the fish from them, and asked “How do you eat them?

S.FORM: Ron̄ “Kmār t-gān qarqar wor ti.”
S.TRANSL: – We just eat them raw.

S.FORM: Magte ron̄ “Ar la ma!” Ni m-la ma, ni so tul leln̄a bnēn.
S.TRANSL: – Let me take them!”, exclaimed the old woman, as she suddenly stuck the fish under her armpit.

S.FORM: Ni m-tul leln̄a bnēn, ni so tul kēl nālman gor.
S.TRANSL: She stuck it under her armpit, and held it with her other hand.

S.FORM: Tōlnēr t-taktak ti; taktak galāg wor, ni m-la kēl dēn o m̄onm̄on leln̄a bnēn, ni m-la ma; ni m-la min rār, titi o law nen̄ va-mnog nok.
S.TRANSL: They all sat there for a little while, going on with their conversation, and finally she took the food parcel from under her arms, and brought it forward. She gave it to the two boys, who saw the fish was now cooked!

S.FORM: Rār m-gān, rār me-tur ma, tōlnēr ra tbirār m-gān, tbirār ron̄: “Ra tbuk, sa gēn vawē le. Kmur m-la o āv sa ave? O va sa me-mnog!”
S.TRANSL: They had a bit of it, and went back home with the rest, so they could share it with their grandfather. As soon as the latter tasted it, he exclaimed: “Hey boys, this is delicious! Where did you find that fire? This food has obviously been cooked!”

S.FORM: Rār ron̄ “Vak sa gin magte.”
S.TRANSL: “We received it from an old woman, over there.” they replied.

S.FORM: Rār / “Ar row kēl, kmur s-la namitōlgēn o āv dēn i magte.” 🌿
S.TRANSL: “Then you should dash back there, and try to steal that woman’s fire for us.” 🌿

S.FORM: Rār m-sur-la kēl vak nen̄, rār m-row sē vak, i magte ni m-to kal nok.
S.TRANSL: Right away they rushed back along the shore – but the old woman had already fled.

S.FORM: Ni m-to srēg tuar masle bē; kma t-var o masle bē nen̄ ti kak ‘Krēwelav’.
S.TRANSL: She was running upriver along a creek, one we call ‘Krēwelav’.

S.FORM: Rār me-tur o vni mtō, rār me-vrisa sag nen̄, rār sur-bē tētēg ni ti; magte so kal le m̄ōs.
S.TRANSL: The two boys grabbed a coconut husk and ran after her, following the creek uphill. But the old woman was already entering the forest.

S.FORM: Rār me-tkar ni sur o āv.
S.TRANSL: They were chasing her to catch her fire.

S.FORM: I magte m-sasiw le masle bē, rār so sasiw le masle bē, magte so kal le m̄ōs.
S.TRANSL: As she waded across the creek, they followed her – but she had already entered the deep forest.

S.FORM: Tōlnēr me-vrisa sag, vrisa sur bē sag avvan, m-dēn̄ o wasn̄in kma t-var ti kak a Nāvnimtō.
S.TRANSL: They ran on and on up along the river, until they reached the place we call Navnimto (‘Coconut Husk’).

S.FORM: Rār me-vrisa vasul ni, rār so qāg tus o vni mtō gor na ngon.
S.TRANSL: As soon as the two boys had overtaken her, they flung their coconut husk at her face.

S.FORM: Magte m-row ma wa magte m-row gās rār, titi o āv so gar gin o vni mtō.
S.TRANSL: The woman managed to jump out and escape them, but the fire had already caught in the husk.

S.FORM: O wasn̄in nen̄, kma t-var ti ron̄ a Nāvnimtō. Namirār o vni mtō t-tog gēs mlē ti, m-ris vāt.
S.TRANSL: Remember we call this place ‘Coconut Husk’. And indeed, the two boys’ coconut husk still exists today, after it turned into a rock.

S.FORM: La rār m-la o āv nen̄, rār so mōl kēl ma sur i tbirār.
S.TRANSL: The boys seized the fire, and brought it back to their grandfather.

S.FORM: Tōlnēr so vōnagav vgar namitōlnēr o āv, tōlnēr t-daw ngatōlnēr o gāngēn ni ti. 🌿
S.TRANSL: The little family was now able to light a fire, which became theirs forever. From that day on, they would always use this fire to cook their food. 🌿

S.FORM: La i magte nen̄ ni m-tur a Nāvnimtō, ni so salvut. Ni m-salvut, ni so row tog mke tuar tōw, kma t-var ti ron̄ “a Mke Grāt”.
S.TRANSL: As for the old woman who was still up at Navnimto, she suddenly took a big leap, and threw herself up to the top of a mountain – the one we call “a-Mke-Ghrāt”.

S.FORM: Ni m-row tog atwal ror, o āv so gān o / o āv m-gān o wavlis, m-gān o dada rga, bas so gān o rga.
S.TRANSL: As soon as she landed, all the vegetation there took fire – grass, leaves, trees, everything was in flames.

S.FORM: Dēkēn, o magte nen̄ ni t-tog t' a Mke Grāt, a mke tōw, o āv t-gān ti, m-gān sursur nok, ni t-tog mlē ti m-dēn̄ naqri. 🌿
S.TRANSL: Up to this day, that old witch still lives on top of Mount Garet. She has consumed that mountain all the way down to its depths, and is still burning today. 🌿

S.FORM: Dōn qōn̄, nēk va-mrōs tektek, nēk s-gav ma mke plēn – oke, nēk s-tek swēl ror: o āv t-qoq ti a mke tōw, kma t-var ti ron̄ a Mke Grāt.
S.TRANSL: One day, if you want to see by yourself, just board a plane, and then look down: you’ll see a cloud of smoke on top of a mountain – that’s our volcano, Mount Ghraat.

S.FORM: Ni me-tger wor nok le tan, titi dēkēn ni t-tog mlēti. O tōw nen̄, kma t-var ti ron̄ a Mke Grāt.
S.TRANSL: She may have sunk into the ground, but she’s still there, inside the volcano.

S.FORM: La magte t-tog t' a Mke Grāt nen̄, ka ni o āv.
S.TRANSL: That old woman inside the volcano is no other than Fire.

S.FORM: Ni m-van dēn a le naw, tāre lōmlōmgāv nen̄ rār me-tkar ni, ni m-to dēn rār.
S.TRANSL: She used to live by the sea, but one day she was chased by two boys and had to run away from them.

S.FORM: Ni gēn so row tog t' a mke tōw nen̄, a Mke Grāt nen̄, ni t-tog mlēti dēn̄ naqri.
S.TRANSL: Eventually she threw herself on to the top of that mountain, Mount Garet, and she still lives there to this day.

S.FORM: Dēkēn, nēr m-lēs tuar sas nen̄ nēr t-var ti ron̄ / leln̄a Waetman, t-var ti ron̄ ‘volkenu’. La le na-ln̄akma, le lanwis, kma t-var ti ron̄ “Mke Grāt”. 🌿
S.TRANSL: Nowadays, some people have adopted a word from the language of Europeans: ‘volkenu’. But in our language, in Dorig, the true name of that mountain is “Mke-Ghraat”, Mount Garet. 🌿

S.FORM: Sususrig sa ni gēn t-bas gēn t' aē sa le.
S.TRANSL: And this is how this story ends.
